label: LIVE CLAUDE

messages_in.content:
TASK
Propose 3 distinct stress scenarios over a horizon of at most 30 days in which the book below loses at least $5,000,000 (a loss means negative total P&L).
Driver family: cold_snap
Season: winter


INPUTS
Context (units: prices $/MWh, gas $/MMBtu, power MW, time days):

  },

   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows below c0",
   "position": "P2",

  },
  {
   "channel": "dart",
   "gains_when": "real-time clears below day-ahead",
   "loses_when": "real-time clears above day-ahead (real-time spikes)",
   "position": "P3",
   "what": "Receives (day-ahead minus real-time) at WEST off-peak on 50 MW (8 h, 24 h on weekends and holidays)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "gas",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price rises relative to gas",
   "loses_when": "scenario losses are measured against the unshocked path (the premium cancels), so P4 loses only when its payoff falls BELOW the unshocked payoff, i.e. when gas rises more than power; it can never lose more than that base payoff",
   "position": "P4",
   "what": "Long heat-rate call on 50 MW, on-peak: pays max(WEST on-peak - 8 x gas - 3, 0) minus a premium of 8.29 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "zone_volume",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens; the loss also grows with load above normal",
   "position": "P5",

  },
  {
   "channel": "tail",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average stays below K6",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average exceeds K6 (price spikes)",
   "position": "P6",
   "what": "Short call on 25 MW of the WEST on-peak daily average, strike K6 = 149.31 $/MWh, premium received 0.53 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  }
 ],
 "book_summary": "P1 (when its size is positive) and P4 are LONG WEST power, so higher WEST prices make them GAIN (a negative P1 size is a SHORT swap that loses when WEST rises); higher gas lowers P4. CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.

scenario.narrative: A persistent 25-day cold spell lifts load to 1.08x normal (load_peak_ratio 1.08) and Henry Hub gas by 30% (gas_hh_pct 30). Winter load raises N.Y.C. demand and its import constraints bind, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is widened by $100/MWh around the clock (pocket_minus_ref_usd 100). The loss comes from P5, the retail load obligation, which is short the spread on about 140 MW or more in all 24 hours. Its estimated loss is about $9.2M, plus a small extra from the higher load. P2 offsets only about $1.5M, and the long WEST positions P1 and P4 gain roughly $0.6M net from the gas and load shocks. I set no WEST on-peak move, no day-ahead/real-time shock, no spikes and no gas basis, because those would mostly help the long WEST positions. Extrapolated linearly from the winter sensitivities, so it is approximate.

A 14-day cold snap raises load to 1.10x normal and Henry Hub gas by 50% (gas_hh_pct 50), with an $8/MMBtu New York gas basis blowout that hits only the heat-rate call P4 (ny_gas_basis_usd 8). N.Y.C. is congested, so the spread widens by $160/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 160), while WEST on-peak softens 30% relative to what gas and load imply (ref_onpeak_pct -30), because upstate is export-constrained and well supplied. This hurts three positions. P5 loses about $8.3M plus about $0.3M from extra load. The WEST price weakness cuts the P1 swap gain, and P4 falls below its unshocked payoff because gas rose more than WEST power. P2 offsets about $1.3M. Net loss is about $7M. Extrapolated linearly and not additive in practice, so the number is approximate.

A severe 8-day arctic outbreak resembling Winter Storm Elliott lifts load to 1.12x normal and gas by 60% (gas_hh_pct 60). Real-time prices clear 30% above day-ahead (dart_pct 30), a mild shock chosen because it also lifts P1. N.Y.C. is cut off from upstate supply, so the spread widens by $280/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 280). Winter Storm Elliott's N.Y.C. minus WEST real-time spread was 338.5 $/MWh (nyc_minus_west_rt_spread_usd_mwh), so this is somewhat below that event. The spread blowout drives the loss: P5 loses about $8.3M plus about $0.2M for load. P3 loses a little from real-time above day-ahead. P2 gains about $1.3M and P1/P4 gain about $0.65M. Net loss is about $6.3M, a linear extrapolation of the winter sensitivities.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A month-long cold regime holds load at 1.03x normal (load_peak_ratio 1.03) and lifts Henry Hub gas by 10% (gas_hh_pct 10). N.Y.C. import limits keep the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread $70/MWh wider for all 30 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 70). WEST on-peak is 20% below what gas and load imply (ref_onpeak_pct -20), because upstate is well supplied and export-limited. The loss is mostly P5, which is short the spread in all 24 hours, roughly $8M over 30 days. P2 recovers about $1.3M. P1 and P4 net to roughly zero or slightly negative because the soft WEST price offsets their gas and load gains. I chose a moderate shock held for a long time to keep the shocks closer to history. The figure is linearly extrapolated from the winter sensitivities, so it is approximate.

A sharp 12-day cold spell lifts load to 1.05x normal (load_peak_ratio 1.05) and Henry Hub gas by 20% (gas_hh_pct 20). A New York gas basis of $5/MMBtu hits only the heat-rate call P4 (ny_gas_basis_usd 5). N.Y.C. is congested, so the spread widens by $170/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 170), while WEST on-peak is 25% below what gas and load imply (ref_onpeak_pct -25). Real-time clears 20% above day-ahead (dart_pct 20), which costs the off-peak DART position P3 a little. The main loss is P5, about $7.9M on the spread and extra load. P2 offsets about $1.1M, and P1 and P4 net a small gain of about $0.2M. The figure is extrapolated linearly from the winter sensitivities, so it is approximate.

A 20-day cold pattern keeps load slightly above normal at 1.04x (load_peak_ratio 1.04) with a small Henry Hub rise of 5% (gas_hh_pct 5). A $3/MMBtu New York gas basis lowers only the P4 payoff (ny_gas_basis_usd 3). The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $90/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd 90), and WEST on-peak falls 35% relative to the gas and load implication (ref_onpeak_pct -35) as upstate supply exceeds what can be exported. This removes most of the gains of the long WEST positions P1 and P4, so their net result is about -$0.5M. P5 loses about $6.9M on the spread and load, and P2 offsets about $1.1M. The net is about a $6M loss. The figure is linearly extrapolated from the winter sensitivities and not additive in practice, so it is approximate.

scenario.narrative: A 15-day summer heat wave lifts the daily peak load to 1.25x a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.25, inside the historical max of 1.514). The N.Y.C. import interface is stressed, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $170/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 170, below the historical max of 289.7). The P5 retail load obligation is short N.Y.C. and hedged only in WEST, so it loses roughly 3,200 $ per $/MWh of spread per day, scaled up by load. P2 (long 25 MW of the spread) offsets about 1.5M. The higher load lifts WEST prices, which helps P1 and P4 by about 1.2M and reduces P5 slightly. Gas, DART, WEST on-peak and spike shocks are set to zero so the loss comes from the zone-volume and congestion channel. Estimate: P5 about -10.1M, P2 about +1.5M, load side effects about +0.7M, net about -7.9M. The estimate is scaled from 5-day sensitivities and is uncertain.

A 25-day summer hot spell raises peak load to 1.15x normal (load_peak_ratio 1.15). Heat-driven demand is concentrated in downstate while upstate WEST stays comparatively well supplied, with strong upstate hydro and imports. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread therefore widens by $120/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 120), which hurts P5 by about 11M; P2 gives back about 1.8M. WEST on-peak prices fall 40% relative to what load implies (ref_onpeak_pct -40). That makes the long WEST swap P1 lose about 0.8M, makes the heat-rate call P4 lose about 0.4M, and lifts the short call P6 slightly. Load effects add back roughly +0.7M. Gas, DART and spikes are zero. This uses the congestion, system and zone-volume channels together. Net estimate is about -9.5M, extrapolated linearly from 5-day sensitivities, so it is uncertain.

A short, intense 8-day summer heat wave, in the style of the June 2025 heat event, pushes load to 1.35x normal (load_peak_ratio 1.35). Local N.Y.C. constraints and real-time scarcity widen the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by $250/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 250, under the historical max of 289.7). This is consistent with the table's N.Y.C. real-time on-peak of 625.5 against WEST at 416.5 on 24 June. P5 loses about 8.6M and P2 recovers about 1.2M. A $2/MMBtu N.Y.C. gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 2) trims the P4 payoff by roughly 0.1M. Load-driven gains in P1 and P4 add about +0.5M. Other shocks are zero. Net estimate is about -7M. The estimate is scaled from 5-day sensitivities and the 250 spread sits close to the historical extreme, so confidence is only medium.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 30-day summer heat season keeps downstate demand elevated. Daily peak load runs at 1.10x a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.10), a moderate shock well inside history. The N.Y.C. import constraint binds persistently, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $75/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 75), far below the historical max of 289.7. The loss comes from P5, the retail load obligation, which is short N.Y.C. and only hedged at WEST, so it loses on every hour of the spread. Calibrating P5 against the earlier runs gives about -8.4M. P2 offsets about +1.35M, and P1 and P4 gain about +1.0M from higher load. Gas, DART, WEST on-peak and spike shocks are zero. Net estimate is about -6.1M. The shocks are small and the duration is long so the loss builds up without a historical outlier. The estimate is scaled from earlier engine results and is uncertain.

A 30-day hot spell concentrates heat in the downstate load pocket while upstate WEST stays well supplied by hydro and imports. Peak load is 1.15x typical (load_peak_ratio 1.15). The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $60/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 60) because of the downstate transfer limit. WEST on-peak prices come in 50% below what load alone implies (ref_onpeak_pct -50), which removes the gains of the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4, so those two positions no longer offset the congestion loss. Estimated P&L: P5 about -7.0M, P2 about +1.1M, P1 and P4 net about -0.4M, so the total is about -6.3M. This combines the zone-volume, system and gas-spread channels. DART, gas and spike shocks are zero. The estimate is scaled from earlier engine results and is uncertain.

A 20-day summer heat episode pushes peak load to 1.15x typical (load_peak_ratio 1.15). Transmission into N.Y.C. is repeatedly congested, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $110/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 110), under the historical max of 289.7. P5, the short N.Y.C. load obligation hedged only at WEST, takes most of the loss, about -8.6M, because its exposure grows with load. P2 offsets about +1.3M and the load-driven gains in P1 and P4 add about +1.0M. WEST on-peak, gas, DART and spike shocks are zero, so the loss is driven by one channel, a pocket-specific squeeze. Net estimate is about -6.3M. The duration is shorter and the spread shock larger than in the 30-day scenarios. The estimate is scaled from earlier engine results and is uncertain.

scenario.narrative: A winter pipeline constraint into downstate New York pushes Henry Hub up 40% and lifts the load peak 5% over a 15-day cold stretch. Gas-fired units in N.Y.C. are marginal and gas-constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $160/MWh on every shocked day. P5 (retail load obligation, short N.Y.C. and hedged only at WEST) loses most of the loss, roughly $9.3M, because the 5% load uplift scales the obligation. P2 recovers about $1.4M of that. The WEST gains on P1 and P4 from higher gas and load are small, about $0.6M. WEST on-peak and DART shocks are zero, so the loss comes from the zone-volume and congestion channels. The estimate scales the supplied 5-day sensitivities linearly, so it is approximate.

A month-long gas supply problem keeps downstate gas tight while upstate is oversupplied. Henry Hub rises 20% and the WEST on-peak price falls a further 20% on top of the gas and load effects, because upstate hydro and import supply dominate. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $70/MWh for 30 days. P5 loses about $7.7M and P2 recovers about $1.3M, so the net is roughly $6.5M. The weaker WEST price costs P1 about $0.5M and P4 gains little because its payoff is eroded as gas rises against power. The small gas-driven gains on P1 offset about $0.4M. Load is unchanged and there are no spikes, so this is a long-duration, congestion-plus-system-level drain rather than a sharp shock. The estimate scales the supplied 5-day sensitivities linearly.

A severe 10-day gas shortage with Henry Hub up 150% and a $10/MMBtu New York gas basis premium hits P4, since the added gas cost lowers the heat-rate call payoff. The load peak rises 8% on cold weather. Gas-fired units downstate set the price while upstate stays comparatively insulated, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $250/MWh, which is inside the winter historical maximum of 400.6. P5 loses about $10M, P2 gains about $1.5M and the higher gas and load lift P1 by about $1M. The net is roughly $7M. A severe, short, high-intensity scenario, driven mainly by zone volume and congestion, with a small headwind on the gas channel. The estimate scales the 5-day sensitivities linearly and is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A month-long winter pipeline constraint keeps downstate gas scarce. Henry Hub rises 30%. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $65/MWh for all 30 days, because N.Y.C. gas-fired units set the price while upstate is comparatively well supplied. The WEST on-peak price falls a further 25% on top of the gas effect, because upstate hydro and imports are plentiful, so P1 and P4 give back their gas gains. Load stays at a normal level, with no spikes and no day-ahead versus real-time shock. P5, which is short N.Y.C. and hedged only at WEST, loses about $7.2M. P2 recovers about $1.2M. P1 and P4 net to roughly -$0.3M. The result is a smaller daily shock held for a long time, which is a lower-severity way to breach the target. The estimate scales the supplied 5-day sensitivities linearly and is approximate.

A 20-day gas supply disruption lifts Henry Hub by 50% and adds a $2/MMBtu New York gas basis premium that raises P4's gas cost. Upstate prices decouple from gas: the WEST on-peak price falls a further 30%, which costs P1 and removes the P4 gains. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $100/MWh because downstate gas units remain marginal. Load is normal and there are no spikes. P5 loses about $7.4M. P2 gains about $1.2M. P1 gains about $0.55M from gas and loses about $0.5M from the weak WEST price. P4 loses its payoff relative to the unshocked path, about $0.15M net. The mix of congestion, system-level and gas channels differs from a pure spread shock. The estimate scales the 5-day sensitivities linearly and is uncertain.

A sharp 8-day downstate gas delivery failure doubles Henry Hub (+100%). The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $280/MWh, which is below the winter historical maximum of 400.6, because N.Y.C. units are forced onto scarce gas while upstate is largely unaffected. Load is normal, WEST on-peak has no extra shock beyond the gas effect, and there are no spikes. P5 loses about $8.3M on the short N.Y.C. retail obligation. P2 recovers about $1.3M, and P1 and P4 gain about $0.5M from the higher WEST price implied by gas. The loss is concentrated in a few days, so this is a short, high-intensity congestion and zone-volume scenario, unlike the long moderate ones. The estimate scales the supplied 5-day sensitivities linearly and is approximate.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A month-long winter gas supply constraint keeps downstate gas scarce while upstate stays well supplied. Henry Hub is unchanged and load is normal. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $55/MWh on all 30 days, because N.Y.C. gas-fired units are marginal and pipeline-limited. The WEST on-peak price falls a further 30% from upstate hydro and import oversupply. P5, short N.Y.C. and hedged only at WEST, loses about $6.1M. P2 recovers about $1.0M. The weak WEST price costs P1 about $0.75M and erodes P4 by about $0.35M. The net is about -$6.2M, a low-level, long-lasting congestion and zone-volume drain with no spikes. The estimate scales the supplied 5-day sensitivities linearly and is approximate.

A 25-day winter gas supply tightness lifts Henry Hub by 10% and adds a $3/MMBtu New York gas basis premium that raises P4's gas cost. Load rises 3% on seasonal cold. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $70/MWh as downstate gas units set the price. The WEST on-peak price falls a further 20% from upstate oversupply. P5 loses about $6.5M and P2 gains about $1.05M. The small gas and load effects lift P1 by about $0.3M, while the weak WEST price takes back about $0.4M on P1 and about $0.2M on P4. The basis premium trims P4 a little more. The net is roughly -$5.8M, driven by zone volume and congestion. The estimate scales the 5-day sensitivities linearly and is uncertain.

A 12-day downstate gas delivery restriction splits the market. Henry Hub is unchanged and load is normal. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $150/MWh, which is well inside the winter historical maximum of 400.6, because N.Y.C. units are forced onto scarce gas while upstate is insulated. The WEST on-peak price falls a further 30% as upstate generation is in surplus. P5 loses about $6.6M on the short N.Y.C. retail obligation. P2 recovers about $1.1M. The weak WEST price costs P1 about $0.3M and erodes P4 by about $0.14M. The net is about -$6.0M, a medium-duration congestion and zone-volume loss with no spikes and no day-ahead versus real-time shock. The estimate scales the 5-day sensitivities linearly and is approximate.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

Load is 6% above a typical winter day on seasonal cold, which scales up the P5 retail obligation. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $75/MWh because downstate gas units set the price. The WEST on-peak price falls a further 35% on upstate oversupply, which cancels the gas and load gains on P1. P5 loses about $7.6M, P2 gains about $1.26M, and P1 and P4 net to about -$0.4M. A 22-day winter gas supply disruption splits the market. Henry Hub rises 15% and a $1/MMBtu New York gas basis premium trims P4's payoff. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $80/MWh because downstate gas units are forced onto scarce gas while upstate is insulated. The WEST on-peak price falls a further 20% on upstate surplus. The net is about -$5.6M, a medium-duration congestion and zone-volume loss with a mild system-level headwind. The estimate scales the sensitivities linearly and is approximate.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Large loads in upstate WEST (data centres, fabs) arrive about 900 MW slower than the Gold Book assumes (large_load_shock_mw -900, load_peak_ratio 0.972, roughly 2.8% of a 31,600 MW normal summer peak). WEST is left long supply, so the WEST on-peak price falls a further 25% (ref_onpeak_pct -25). N.Y.C. is export-constrained and its prices do not fall with WEST, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $70/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 70). This persists for 30 days. P5 (short N.Y.C. load, long WEST hedge) loses on the wider spread, which outweighs the P2 gain. The lower WEST price also hurts P1 and P4. Gas, DART and spike shocks are left at zero. The loss estimate is scaled linearly from the 5-day sensitivities, so it is uncertain.

A near-term large-load shortfall of 500 MW (large_load_shock_mw -500, load_peak_ratio 0.984) removes upstate WEST demand but leaves the N.Y.C. pocket tight. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $85/MWh for the full 30 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 85), inside the historical summer maximum of 289.7. The loss comes mainly from the congestion and zone-volume channel. P5, short about 140 MW of N.Y.C. load against a WEST hedge, loses far more than the P2 long spread gains, a net of about $2.6k per day for each $1/MWh of widening. WEST price, gas, DART and spike shocks are zero, so the P1, P4 and P6 effects are small. The loss estimate is scaled from the 5-day sensitivities.

A deep 2035-style shortfall of 1,400 MW in new large loads (large_load_shock_mw -1400, load_peak_ratio 0.956) coincides with soft gas, Henry Hub down 35% (gas_hh_pct -35). The WEST on-peak price falls a further 20% (ref_onpeak_pct -20) on weak demand, which hurts the long WEST positions P1 and P4. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $60/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 60) because N.Y.C. stays constrained. This lasts 30 days. The main loss is P5 on the wider spread, with the WEST price decline on P1 and P4 adding to it. The loss estimate is uncertain because P4 is floored at its base payoff and effects are not additive.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

Henry Hub rises 30% (gas_hh_pct 30), for example from a supply issue unrelated to load. The WEST on-peak price still falls a further 30% (ref_onpeak_pct -30), so power falls while gas rises. This squeezes the heat rate and wipes out the P4 payoff, while P1 loses on the lower WEST price and is only partly cushioned by the gas pass-through. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $55/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 55), and P5 loses on this over 30 days. The estimate is uncertain because the shocks are not additive and P4 is floored.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Large loads arrive about 200 MW slower than forecast (large_load_shock_mw -200, load_peak_ratio 0.995), a small shortfall that barely changes the system balance. N.Y.C. stays export-constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $66/MWh for the full 30 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 66). This is the main loss channel. P5, short about 140 MW of N.Y.C. load against a WEST hedge, loses on the wider spread, and P2 offsets only part of it. WEST on-peak prices ease a further 12% (ref_onpeak_pct -12), which adds modest losses on P1 and P4. Gas, DART and spike shocks are zero. The loss estimate is scaled from the earlier engine results, so it is uncertain.

Large loads arrive about 917 MW slower than the Gold Book assumes (large_load_shock_mw -917, load_peak_ratio 0.971), leaving upstate WEST with surplus supply. This scenario works mainly through the system channel. WEST on-peak prices fall a further 60% (ref_onpeak_pct -60), inside the historical summer minimum of -88.5%. This hits the long WEST swap P1 and wipes out most of the P4 heat-rate call payoff. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by a moderate $45/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 45), so P5 adds a loss that P2 only partly offsets. The scenario lasts 30 days. Gas, DART and spike shocks are zero. The estimate is uncertain because the shocks are not additive and P4 is floored at its base payoff.

A near-term shortfall of 500 MW in large loads (large_load_shock_mw -500, load_peak_ratio 0.984) leaves the system slack. Real-time prices clear 40% below day-ahead (dart_pct -40) as forecast load is not met. This lowers the realised WEST price, so the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4 lose. P3 and P6 gain a little, which only partly offsets that. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $62/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 62), so P5 takes the main loss and P2 offsets about a fifth of it. The scenario lasts 30 days. The WEST on-peak move, gas and spike shocks are zero. The estimate is scaled from the 5-day sensitivities and is uncertain.
